lessons.title: ഹൃദയം (hṛdayaṁ) — "heart," a cousin of the English word
lessons.gloss: heart — Sanskrit tatsama, and a genuine (if distant) cousin of the English word

segments.text: Suhṛttŭ, "friend," was built on hṛd, "heart" — a piece promised, not yet taught. Here it is, whole.

ഹൃദയം (hṛdayaṁ) is Sanskrit हृदय (hṛdaya), "heart," absorbed with the same nativizing ‑അം you already met on കുടുംബം and ഇഷ്ടം. Its root, हृद् (hṛd), is not just Indo-Aryan but Indo-European: the same ancient root that gave Greek kardía, Latin cor/cordis, and — by a long chain of regular sound changes inside Germanic — English heart itself. Hṛdayaṁ and "heart" are genuine cousins, distant but real, through Sanskrit's own branch of the family tree English belongs to. That resemblance is a coincidence of deep history, not of Malayalam's own Dravidian family — Dravidian and Indo-European share no common ancestor at all.
Suhṛttŭ, "friend," is this very root wearing "good" in front of it — su + hṛd, good-heart.

segments.text: Say "my heart." (Ente hṛdayaṁ.) Is hṛdayaṁ a Dravidian word or a Sanskrit one? (Sanskrit, dressed in Malayalam's own ‑aṁ.) Name an English word that is a genuine, if distant, cousin of hṛd. (Heart — both from the same PIE root, by way of Greek kardía and Latin cor.) Which earlier word was built on this same root? (സുഹൃത്ത് — su "good" + hṛd "heart.")

lessons.title: നെഞ്ച് (nenchŭ) — "chest," Malayalam's other heart
lessons.gloss: chest — Malayalam's other heart, native this time, and the one everyday idiom reaches for

segments.text: ഹൃദയം (hṛdayaṁ) was borrowed, formal, and shared with English by deep ancestry. This chapter's second word is none of those three things.

നെഞ്ച് (nenchŭ) is native Dravidian, cognate with Tamil's own நெஞ்சு/நெஞ்சம் (nenju/nenjam), "chest." Where ഹൃദയം (hṛdayaṁ) names the organ and carries the Sanskrit-flavoured abstraction — a "heartfelt" thank-you, a broken heart in the literary sense — നെഞ്ച് (nenchŭ) is the word everyday idiom actually reaches for: നെഞ്ചിടിപ്പ് (nenchiṭippŭ), a heart pounding from fear or excitement, literally "chest-beat."

Two hearts, then: one Sanskrit and formal, one native and physical. That is the same selective-borrowing pattern Chapter 2 already showed with സന്തോഷം beside നന്ദി — Malayalam does not simply prefer Sanskrit or prefer native; it keeps both, and lets register decide which one a given sentence reaches for. തല and കൈ, this stretch's first two body words, were native throughout; ഹൃദയം (hṛdayaṁ) and നെഞ്ച് (nenchŭ) show the same body carrying one word of each kind, side by side.

segments.text: Say "my chest." (Ente nenchŭ.) Which of this chapter's two heart-words is native, and which is borrowed? (നെഞ്ച് native; ഹൃദയം (hṛdayaṁ) Sanskrit.) What does nenchiṭippŭ mean, literally? ("Chest-beat" — a pounding heart.) Which earlier pair showed this same native-plus-Sanskrit side-by-side pattern? (സന്തോഷം beside നന്ദി, Chapter 2.)
